title: Microgateway onramp cheat notes (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope

This is a lightweight, pragmatic lab-style cheat sheet for teams that want to put Redwood inference behind a microgateway (sidecar or API-proxy) as a fast onramp. Audience: platform engineers, backend engineers integrating LLM calls from microservices, and SDK/infra folks trying to standardize per-service adapters.

Why this exists (short):
- Many teams prefer a tiny gateway that centralizes auth, retries, caching, and per-tenant routing rather than calling Redwood directly from each service.
- This doc captures a minimal working pattern, common gotchas, and quick troubleshooting heuristics so integrators can ship in 1–2 days and avoid easy production mistakes.

High-level pattern

1) Service -> Microgateway (sidecar/proxy)
2) Microgateway handles: auth headers, feature flags (model selection), batching, KV/prefix caching, rate-limits and fallback rules
3) Microgateway -> Redwood API (hosted/dedicated/private)

Minimum requirements for the microgateway

- HTTP/2 or keepalive-enabled HTTP/1.1 to avoid excessive TLS handshakes.
- Short-circuit cache for repeated prompts (cache key = model + prompt-hash + ctx-length).
- Simple request queue + batcher (configurable window = 6–25ms).
- Transparent propagation of request metadata: x-rw-org-id, x-rw-route-id, x-rw-request-id.
- Token rotation: integrate with vault/KMS for service account keys.

Env vars and config example (minimal)

RW_UPSTREAM=https://api.redwood-inference.com
RW_API_KEY_SECRET_PATH=secret/data/team/infra/redwood-api-key
BATCH_WINDOW_MS=10
BATCH_MAX_TOKENS=2048
CACHE_TTL_MS=60000
DEFAULT_MODEL=redwood-1-small
FALLBACK_MODEL=redwood-1-fast

Sample curl through proxy (smoke test)

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"prompt":"Summarize the last deploy in 2 lines","max_tokens":60}'

Expect 200 json. If 401 -> check RW_API_KEY secret mount; if 502/504 -> check network + keepalive + upstream health.

Node.js minimal adapter snippet (conceptual)

// pseudo-code: keep it tiny
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
async function callUpstream(body, traceHeaders) {
  const res = await fetch(process.env.RW_UPSTREAM + '/v1/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: Object.assign({'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, traceHeaders),
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
    keepalive: true // runtime hint
  });
  return res.json();
}

Batching behavior notes

- Batch window: aim for 8–15ms for interactive UIs, 20–30ms for background jobs. Lower window -> lower latency but higher cost.
- Batch formation key: model + org_id + decoding-mode. Do NOT batch across different decoding modes (e.g., streaming + non-streaming).
- Measure: batch size histogram (helpful for cost attribution).

Auth & multi-tenant patterns

- Prefer a single long-lived service token for the microgateway; Redwood usage then attributed to the gateway route. Use RBAC and per-route tags to break down cost.
- If customers require per-tenant keys, implement token binding in the gateway: fetch tenant key via KMS per incoming request and inject x-rw-org-id. Cache tenant keys for TTL (60s).

Telemetry + dashboards (quick)

Essential metrics to emit from the gateway:
- upstream_call_latency_p50/p95/p99 (ms)
- local_queue_depth (gauge)
- batch_size_histogram
- upstream_5xx_rate and upstream_429_rate
- token_consumption_per_route (tokens/min)
- cache_hit_ratio
- open_stream_count (for streaming endpoints)

Recommended dashboards: per-route p95 vs Redwood upstream p95, cost per 1k tokens, batch size over time, cache hit ratio. Hook gateways trace ids to Redwood request logs (x-rw-request-id) for end-to-end traces.

Common failure modes & quick fixes

1) Latency spikes after deploy
- Cause: warmstart cold kernels on dedicated pools or Java GC in gateway.
- Quick fix: add a warmup runner (small request every 10s) or use keepalive pools. Check p95 bulk from Redwood console.

2) 401s intermittently
- Cause: secret rotation or missing header injection.
- Quick fix: validate secret mount path, test the gateway's secret refresh logic. Log the token fingerprint (not token) for correlation.

3) 502/504 when traffic increases
- Cause: upstream connection limits or blocked egress, or batching deadlock.
- Quick fix: ensure connection pool size > anticipated concurrency, enable http2, inspect gateway health and upstream logs.

4) Streaming endpoints hang or early-close
- Cause: proxy trimming trailing newlines or buffering at LB.
- Quick fix: ensure transfer-encoding: chunked passthrough and disable response buffering in gateway (Nginx proxy_buffering off / envoy streaming config).

Operational checklist before pilot (minimal)

- [ ] Confirm RW_UPSTREAM and auth mode (service token vs per-tenant).
- [ ] Add telemetry exporters (Prometheus + traces) and a basic dashboard template.
- [ ] Create a smoke test that runs on deploy and verifies generate + streaming + embeddings end-to-end.
- [ ] Set circuit breaker: fail open for non-critical routes with fallback_model configured.
- [ ] Add per-route cost tags to enable token-level breakdown in Redwood Console.

Safety and privacy notes

- Do not log raw prompts. Always hash prompt snippets before writing to logs. If inspection is required, store an encrypted blob with access audit and TTL.
- For PII workflows, prefer Private deployments or dedicated pools and route via on-prem microgateway that never egresses to hosted.

Quick reference: fallback policy example (YAML)

fallbacks:
  - when: upstream_5xx_rate > 0.02
    action: switch_model
    to: redwood-1-fast
    reason: emergency_cost-latency-fallback

Open questions (to resolve in next sync)

- Should per-service adapters surface token-level cost in the gateway logs or rely on Redwood Console attribution? (tradeoff: instrumentation complexity vs. visibility)
- Recommended default batch window across web vs background workloads: can we define a company standard?
- How to best support function-calling semantics through the gateway with minimal schema translation?

Next steps (owner: Jordan Le)

1) Prototype: ship a tiny Go + Envoy example repo that has the essential pieces (batcher, cache, keeper for secrets). Target: 2-day prototype. PR: link in linked_artifacts.
2) Ramp: onboard 2 internal teams as pilots (search bot, support-assistant).
3) Docs: merge this cheat sheet into the onramp cookbook and add a diagram + sample dashboards.

Meeting notes (2026-02-10 sync)

- Ava: wants a per-route telemetry contract and a small Prometheus client lib.
- Diego: will prototype the keepalive pool logic and run load tests.
- Priya: will draft compliance language about logging and PII for the cookbook.

Notes to self (quick):
- keep the adapter surface minimal: generate(), stream(), embed() endpoints only.
- prefer transparent tracing headers so we can tie to Redwood console traces.
- when in doubt, fail to simple fallback rather than block caller.

If you take this and run a quick prototype, ping #devexp-onramp with the repo link and we'll pair on a pilot.
